design_detail: Twenty-day within-participant double-blind residential laboratory study in 9 men, run in three groups of three or four. Four 5-day blocks, one per drug condition: oral methamphetamine 10 mg with a placebo drink, methamphetamine 10 mg with alcohol 0.375 g/kg, methamphetamine 10 mg with alcohol 0.75 g/kg, and a placebo capsule with alcohol 0.75 g/kg; there was no placebo-plus-placebo condition. Within each block, day 1 was a placebo baseline, active drug was given three times (morning and evening of day 2 and evening of day 3), placebo was given on the morning of day 3 and on days 4-5. Capsules were given at 0900 and 2100 h and drinks an hour later. Breath alcohol, blood pressure, heart rate, mood ratings and a five-task cognitive battery were measured repeatedly; sleep was measured each night by actigraphy and a morning questionnaire; social behaviour and cigarette use were recorded. The tolerance analysis compares the first administration (day 2 morning) with the third (day 3 evening). Dosing order was counterbalanced so that no two people had the same condition in the same block.
can_establish: How a single oral dose of methamphetamine, alcohol and their combination differ on heart rate, blood pressure, mood ratings, performance and sleep in the same men; and whether those differences are smaller by the third administration of the same combination within about 36 hours.
cannot_establish: Cross-tolerance between the two drugs in the usual sense (no condition tested one drug after a course of the other); what happens at the doses and routes of non-medical methamphetamine use; effects in people who use methamphetamine regularly, since only one of the nine reported current methamphetamine use; and whether a smaller third response is tolerance rather than an effect of time of day or of the previous night's lost sleep, a limitation the authors state.

sample.recruitment: Adults who used stimulants and alcohol, recruited by word of mouth and by newspaper and online advertisement in New York City (Methods > Participants, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: At least 21 years old, past-year use of amphetamine, methamphetamine or MDMA and current (past 30 days) alcohol use; excluded for significant medical history (cardiovascular, neurological or major psychiatric illness, other than stimulant dependence) or any condition increasing the risk of participation.
sample.demographics: Nine men (six Black, one Hispanic, two White), mean age 41.1 years (SD 3.9), 13.6 years of education (SD 1.6), body mass index 26.4 (SD 3.5). All drank alcohol currently (1-5 days a week, 3-7 drinks a day) and all used cocaine currently (1-6 days a week); two used cannabis, one used methamphetamine (3 days a week), six smoked 5-10 cigarettes a day and eight used caffeine. Three met criteria for cocaine dependence; none was seeking treatment and none met criteria for any other Axis I disorder.
sample.attrition: None reported: nine men completed the 20-day study.
sample.selection_effects: Men only, middle-aged, all drinking currently and all using cocaine currently, recruited in one city for a 20-day residential stay at $70 a day. Only one reported current methamphetamine use, which the authors name as an important limitation for the sleep findings; alcohol tolerance is likely in a sample drinking 3-7 drinks a day.

exposure.measurement: Drug given under supervision in a private vestibule and measured for alcohol by breath analyser at baseline and 0.75, 1.5, 2.25, 3, 4, 5 and 6 hours after the capsule; methamphetamine concentrations were not measured.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral methamphetamine hydrochloride (Desoxyn tablets repackaged in opaque capsules with lactose) at 10 mg or placebo, and a 500 mL drink containing vodka at 0.375 or 0.75 g/kg of estimated total body water, or a matched placebo drink, both topped with 1 mL of vodka and a drop of peppermint oil and matched for calories. Three active administrations per block (day 2 morning, day 2 evening, day 3 evening).
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol is itself one of the study conditions. Tobacco was available from 0800 to 2330 h and cigarette counts were analysed; the authors report that cigarette consumption did not affect the drug results, while the combination with the larger alcohol dose raised consumption by about 4-5 cigarettes a day. No other drugs were available during the residential stay; current cocaine use by all participants and cocaine dependence in three are background characteristics, not exposures during the study.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Residential confinement for 20 days with placebo baseline and washout days in each block; no biological verification of abstinence from other drugs is described. Before enrolment each person received 10 mg methamphetamine with the largest alcohol dose on an outpatient day, so the first in-study administration was not the first exposure to the combination.

comparison.controls: Within-person: the placebo baseline day of each block, the placebo mornings and washout days, and the other three drug conditions. Methamphetamine alone and alcohol alone each serve as the comparator for the combination; there was no placebo-plus-placebo condition, which the authors justify by the study's aim and the time burden.
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover with counterbalanced dosing order across blocks, so that no two participants received the same condition in the same block.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable: every comparison is within person.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no separate control group); all participants used cocaine currently, which is a feature of the sample rather than a between-group difference.

outcomes.instruments: A computerized 100-mm visual analogue mood questionnaire; a drug-effect questionnaire rating good and bad effects and drug strength 0-4, desire to take the drug again, and liking from -4 to +4; a five-task cognitive battery (digit recall, digit-symbol substitution, divided attention, rapid information processing, repeated acquisition); blood pressure and heart rate; breath alcohol; Actiwatch actigraphy giving total sleep time, sleep-onset latency, sleep efficiency and wake bouts, with a morning sleep questionnaire; computer-prompted observation of social behaviour every 2.5 minutes; cigarette counts.
outcomes.validity_norms: Established laboratory instruments for this group; actigraphy is a movement-based estimate of sleep rather than polysomnography, and the mood scales have no external norms.
outcomes.operationalization: Tolerance is operationalized as a significant fall in the area under the effect-time curve from the first to the third administration of the same condition, tested as a drug condition by administration-number interaction with planned comparisons.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None at the family level: two-factor repeated-measures analyses of variance with planned between-drug and within-drug comparisons, p<0.05, with Huynh-Feldt corrections where appropriate. Tables 3, 4 and 5 report fifteen, five and fourteen outcomes respectively, each with three or four comparisons.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind for the capsule; participants were told the study concerned alcohol and an approved stimulant or sedative. Alcohol itself cannot be blinded in people who drink regularly, and ratings of 'drunk' differed sharply by condition, so blinding of the alcohol conditions cannot be assumed; blinding integrity was not tested.

analysis.effect_sizes: Effect sizes labelled d are given for every comparison alongside F values, with means and standard errors in Tables 3-5. Degrees of freedom are consistent with nine participants throughout (F 21,168 for the four-condition by eight-time-point acute analyses, F 3,24 for the tolerance analyses, F 18,144 for performance, F 12,96 for sleep and residual effects, F 12,60 for cigarettes in the six smokers). The printed d values reach 33.3 for breath alcohol and 6.7-33.3 across the alcohol comparisons, which cannot be conventional between-group standardized differences; the paper does not say how they were computed, so they should be read as within-person standardized values from the analysis-of-variance error term and not compared with Cohen's benchmarks (editors' note).
analysis.covariates: None; within-person analyses of variance with planned comparisons.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the New York State Psychiatric Institute.
analysis.selective_reporting: Peak cardiovascular and subjective data are said to be reported in Table 3 only 'for the sake of brevity'; several analyses are reported as 'data not shown' (cigarette comparisons between conditions); the sleep and residual tables report only the measures that reached significance.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation and no power statement; nine men, every effect tested within person. The authors attribute some null findings to the sample and note that most participants did not use methamphetamine regularly.

interpretation_gap.results_show: At the first administration, the combination raised heart rate and ratings of 'good drug effect' more than either drug alone; methamphetamine reduced alcohol-related performance decrements and ratings of 'drunk' and 'sedated'; and the larger alcohol dose blunted methamphetamine's disruption of sleep. By the third administration, about 36 hours later, the heart-rate and 'good drug effect' advantages of the combination were significantly smaller and no longer differed from alcohol alone, while blood-pressure effects were unchanged. Residual next-day effects were few.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says that by the third administration many of these effects were significantly diminished, 'suggesting that participants developed tolerance', and the discussion repeats this while listing two alternatives in the same paragraph: the first administration was in the morning and the third in the evening, and the third followed a night of drug-disrupted sleep. The data show a smaller response at the third administration; the study design does not separate tolerance from time of day or from accumulated sleep loss, and the authors say so. The conclusion that the combination's profile explains why the drugs are used together is an interpretation, since no self-administration or choice measure was taken.

timeline.event: Single-dose intravenous methamphetamine 30 mg with oral alcohol 1 g/kg: greater heart-rate rise and euphoria than either drug alone, and less subjective intoxication, with no performance effects (Mendelson et al., 1995)
Three days of twice-daily oral methamphetamine in the same residential laboratory: tolerance to positive subjective ratings and to sleep disruption across days
Thirteen days of daily oral methamphetamine: a smaller heart-rate response to a fixed challenge afterwards

replication.where_it_stands: The acute interaction (greater heart rate and euphoria, less felt intoxication) agrees with the one earlier human study of this combination and with studies of alcohol combined with cocaine, caffeine and d-amphetamine. The loss of those effects by a third administration within 36 hours is reported here alone; the same laboratory had previously found tolerance to positive subjective effects of methamphetamine alone across three days.

funding.funder: Grant DA-03746 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported in the PubMed Central author manuscript: no competing-interests statement appears.
funding.affiliations_note: Columbia University and the New York State Psychiatric Institute; the same laboratory and the same grant number as Comer et al. (2001), so the two studies are not independent replications of one another.

what_would_settle_it: A residential study giving the same methamphetamine-alcohol combination at the same time of day on several consecutive days, with a placebo-plus-placebo condition, sleep held constant or measured as a mediator, plasma methamphetamine concentrations, and people who use methamphetamine regularly, so that a smaller later response can be attributed to tolerance rather than to time of day or lost sleep.

domains.domain: Randomization process (counterbalanced order of the four blocks)
domains.note: Dosing order was counterbalanced so that no two participants had the same condition in the same block, but the method of allocation is not described and no period effect is reported.

Blocks were separated by placebo washout days and residual effects were measured and were small, but within a block the three administrations fall in about 36 hours and the tolerance comparison is between a morning dose and an evening dose two nights later, with the second night's sleep disturbed by the drug.

The capsule was double-blind, but alcohol at 0.75 g/kg in men who drink 3-7 drinks a day is recognizable: ratings of 'drunk' reached 44.2 under alcohol alone against 1.1 under methamphetamine alone. Blinding integrity was not assessed, and the main outcomes are self-rated.
All nine men completed the 20-day protocol and no missing data are reported.

Breath alcohol, cardiovascular measures, actigraphy and performance are objective; the tolerance outcomes that carry the conclusion are self-rated mood scales, and sleep is estimated from movement rather than polysomnography.

No protocol or pre-specified primary outcome; roughly sixty outcomes with uncorrected planned comparisons; peak data confined to a table 'for the sake of brevity'; several analyses reported as data not shown; and the significance footnotes of Tables 3 and 4 do not define all the markers used.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A 20-day within-person residential design with four conditions, counterbalanced order and objective measurement of alcohol, sleep and performance is a strong way to study a drug combination, and the degrees of freedom check out against the sample size throughout. The overall judgment is set by the blinding of the alcohol conditions and by the number of uncorrected comparisons behind the subjective findings. The source can be cited for the acute interaction between oral methamphetamine and alcohol on heart rate, mood and performance, for the attenuation of methamphetamine's sleep disruption by alcohol, and for the observation that these differences were smaller by a third administration; it cannot be cited for cross-tolerance between the drugs, for doses and routes used outside the laboratory, or for effects in people who use methamphetamine regularly.

key_findings.finding: At the first administration the combination raised heart rate more than either drug alone, and the larger alcohol dose more than the smaller (F 21,168 = 10.9-30.2, p<0.005 for all comparisons, d = 1.5-2.3). All active conditions raised heart rate above baseline; methamphetamine-containing conditions raised systolic pressure and the combinations raised diastolic pressure, while alcohol alone did not significantly raise blood pressure.
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute effects (day 2) > Cardiovascular effects, whole subsection; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: By the third administration the heart-rate advantage of the combination had shrunk: both combinations produced significantly smaller heart-rate area-under-curve values at administration 3 than at administration 1 (F 3,24 = 15.4-26.5, p<0.0001, d = 0.8-1.6), and only the larger-alcohol combination still exceeded methamphetamine alone and alcohol alone (F 3,24 = 11.3-14.5, p<0.005, d = 0.7-0.9). Blood-pressure effects were unchanged across administrations.
key_findings.locator: Results > Tolerance > Cardiovascular and BAL effects, whole subsection; Figure 4 (left panel)

key_findings.finding: The same pattern appeared in the wanted subjective effects. At administration 1 the larger-alcohol combination produced higher 'good drug effect' and lower 'drunk' ratings than alcohol alone (F 3,24 = 10.7-12.7, p<0.005, d = 0.6-0.8); by administration 3 neither differed from alcohol alone, and 'good drug effect' area-under-curve values were significantly smaller at administration 3 than at administration 1 for both combinations (F 3,24 = 12.1-14.9, p<0.005, d = 0.7-0.8).
key_findings.locator: Results > Tolerance > Subjective effects, whole subsection; Figure 4 (middle and right panels)

key_findings.finding: Table 4 gives the size of the fall for the larger-alcohol combination between the first and third administration: 'content' from 122.6 (SEM 40.3) to 72.6 (SEM 26.1), 'energetic' from 118.2 (SEM 31.5) to 70.1 (SEM 23.0), 'high' from 96.6 (SEM 27.0) to 56.0 (SEM 18.3), drug-effect-questionnaire 'good drug effect' from 4.8 (SEM 0.9) to 3.2 (SEM 0.6) and drug liking from 3.1 (SEM 1.7) to 1.1 (SEM 1.5), all significant against the same condition's first administration. Under alcohol alone, 'energetic' (112.6 to 40.0) and drug liking (3.6 to 1.3) also fell significantly.
key_findings.locator: Table 4, visual analogue scale and drug-effects-questionnaire rows

key_findings.finding: At the first administration the combination produced larger increases in 'good drug effect' than either drug alone (F 21,168 = 12.5-52.0, p<0.05, d = 1.0-2.0), while alcohol alone produced the highest ratings of 'drunk' (peak 44.2, SEM 13.5, against 13.9 for the larger-alcohol combination and 1.1 for methamphetamine alone) and of 'sedated' (34.3 against 10.6 and 3.3).
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute effects (day 2) > Subjective effects, 1st paragraph; Table 3, peak subjective-effect ratings

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine blunted alcohol's effect on performance: alcohol alone reduced maximum tracking speed on the divided-attention task compared with every other condition (F 18,144 = 6.3-12.9, p<0.05, d = 2.4-2.7) and reduced hits on the rapid information task compared with methamphetamine alone (F 18,144 = 6.7, p<0.05, d = 1.3), while the combinations produced no such decrements. The combination with the larger alcohol dose did raise errors on the repeated-acquisition task compared with methamphetamine alone and with the smaller-alcohol combination (F 18,144 = 14.4-18.2, p<0.001, d = 1.5-1.7).
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute effects (day 2) > Cognitive/psychomotor performance effects, whole subsection; Figure 3

key_findings.finding: Alcohol softened methamphetamine's disruption of sleep. On the night of day 2, all methamphetamine conditions reduced hours slept and sleep efficiency compared with alcohol alone (F 12,96 = 11.6-30.7, p<0.005, d = 1.2-2.5), and methamphetamine alone reduced both more than the combination with the larger alcohol dose (F 12,96 = 4.6, p<0.05, d = 0.7-0.8); the same pattern appeared in estimated hours slept and ratings of sleeping well. Sleep-onset latency was 53.4 minutes (SEM 13.1) after methamphetamine alone against 20.6 (SEM 3.9) after alcohol alone, with 6.9 awakenings an hour against 3.5.
key_findings.locator: Results > Sleep effects, whole subsection; Table 5, sleep questionnaire and Actiwatch rows; Figure 5

key_findings.finding: Residual effects the next day were few: heart rate was still slightly raised on day 3 by methamphetamine alone and by the larger-alcohol combination compared with alcohol alone (F 12,96 = 7.3-19.4, p<0.01, d = 0.5-0.8), ratings of 'upset stomach' were higher and ratings of 'tired' higher after methamphetamine alone, and there were no residual effects on any cognitive or psychomotor task.
key_findings.locator: Results > Residual effects > Cardiovascular effects and Subjective effects; Results > Residual effects > Cognitive/psychomotor performance effects; Figure 6; Table 5

key_findings.finding: The combination with the larger alcohol dose increased cigarette smoking among the six smokers by about 4-5 cigarettes a day (9.5, SEM 1.4, against 14.2, SEM 1.9; F 12,60 = 24.1, p<0.05, d = 0.9) and more than every other condition, and participants spent a smaller share of their social time talking after methamphetamine alone (10.9%) than under any alcohol condition (24.8-28.5%).
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute effects (day 2) > Effects of cigarette smoking and > Effects on social interactions

reporting_issues.issue: Tables 3, 4 and 5 use four and five asterisks on several entries, but their footnotes define only one, two and three asterisks (significantly different from methamphetamine alone, from the smaller-alcohol combination and from the larger-alcohol combination; and in Table 4 from the first and third administrations of alcohol alone and the first of the combination).
reporting_issues.locator: Table 3 footnotes and rows 'Good drug effect', 'High', 'Mellow', 'Stimulated', 'Drunk'; Table 4 footnotes and row 'Content'; Table 5 footnotes and rows 'Fell asleep easily', 'Headache'
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison that each marked entry refers to cannot be determined from the table alone; where an entry carries an undefined marker, the claim should rest on the comparisons stated in the running text instead.

reporting_issues.issue: The effect sizes printed as d reach 33.3 for breath alcohol and run from 6.7 to 33.3 across the alcohol comparisons, with values of 2.1-3.3 for heart rate against baseline; no formula is given.
reporting_issues.locator: Results > Acute effects (day 2) > Breath alcohol levels and > Cardiovascular effects
reporting_issues.consequence: These cannot be read as conventional standardized mean differences, where values above about 2 are already very large. Any claim citing this study should quote the means and standard errors in the tables rather than the d values.

reporting_issues.issue: The tolerance comparison is between the first administration, given at 0900 h on day 2, and the third, given at 2100 h on day 3; the discussion names time of day and the previous night's drug-disturbed sleep as alternative explanations, but the abstract states only that tolerance developed.
reporting_issues.locator: Methods and materials > Design; Abstract; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader taking the abstract alone would treat a morning-to-evening comparison after a disturbed night as a clean measure of tolerance. The claim should say that the response was smaller at the third administration and that the design cannot separate tolerance from time of day or sleep loss.

reporting_issues.issue: There is no placebo-plus-placebo condition, so no measurement in these men is free of both drugs apart from the baseline day of each block.
reporting_issues.locator: Methods and materials > Procedure > Drug, last paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Every reported effect of methamphetamine alone is against alcohol alone or against the block's baseline day, not against a double placebo; the size of each drug's effect cannot be separated from the other's absence in the within-day comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: Each participant received 10 mg methamphetamine with the largest alcohol dose on an outpatient day before enrolment, to check for adverse reactions and to give them experience of the combination.
reporting_issues.consequence: The first in-study administration was not the first exposure to the combination, so any tolerance measured from it starts from an already exposed state.

reporting_issues.issue: Only one of the nine participants reported current methamphetamine use, while all nine used cocaine currently and three met criteria for cocaine dependence; the abstract describes the sample only as 'nine adult male volunteers'.
reporting_issues.locator: Methods and materials > Participants, 2nd paragraph; Table 1; Discussion, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample's stimulant experience is mostly with cocaine, which the authors name as a limitation for the sleep findings; results should not be transferred to people who use methamphetamine regularly.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3220757 (author manuscript of Psychopharmacology 2011;219(1):191-204), read in the browser pane; tables 1-5 render as text and were read in full, figures 1-6 are images and no values were taken from them. Supplementary material: none offered.
